title: What a translation claims
bodyMd:
Every argument about translation eventually reaches the same impasse. One party insists that a translator's duty is to the author: the words chosen, the order in which they arrive, the strangeness of an unfamiliar idiom, are all part of what was written, and to smooth them away is to substitute one's own book for someone else's. The other party insists that the duty is to the reader: a sentence that was fluent in its own language and is laboured in the new one has not been preserved but damaged, since fluency was among the things the original possessed.

Stated that way the dispute looks unresolvable, because each side is describing a real loss. It becomes more tractable if one notices an assumption both sides share: that there exists, in the original, a fixed quantity of meaning which the translation either transmits or fails to transmit. Drop that assumption and the question changes. A translation is then not a container of greater or lesser leakage but a reading — one defensible performance of a text among several — and the relevant question is not how much was lost but what this particular reading makes newly audible.

This is not a licence for invention. A reading can be wrong: it can rest on a misconstrued grammar, or on an idiom the translator did not recognise, and such errors are correctable by ordinary scholarly means. What a mistaken reading is not, once we abandon the fixed-quantity picture, is a deviation from a single authorised version that a sufficiently careful translator could have reproduced. The honest claim a translator can make is therefore narrower than fidelity and more demanding than taste: that this reading can be defended from the text.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage of about 300 words on the philosophy of translation. The first paragraph sets out two opposed positions: that the translator owes a duty to the author and must keep the original wording and strangeness, and that the translator owes a duty to the reader and must keep the original fluency. The second paragraph identifies an assumption both positions share, namely that the original contains a fixed quantity of meaning that the translation transmits or loses, and proposes dropping it so that a translation counts as one defensible reading among several. The third paragraph denies that this licenses invention, allows that a reading can be wrong through misconstrued grammar or an unrecognised idiom, and concludes that the honest claim a translator can make is that the reading can be defended from the text.

provenance.notes: Original argumentative prose written for this question bank. It states a general position in translation theory in the author’s own words; no published essay, book or article was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed.
